title: Net-shape additive manufacturing of fully dense technical ceramics

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a ceramic printing process family that combines complex geometry, conventional sintered density and strength, and final dimensions accurate enough for functional surfaces to be used without finish grinding. Target materials include alumina, zirconia, silicon carbide and silicon nitride. The central capability is to achieve these properties together, including in parts with enclosed channels or other features inaccessible to machining.

Here, net shape means meeting the intended application's final dimensional requirements. It does not require literally zero dimensional change during processing. Likewise, fully dense must be assessed through measured density and residual porosity, rather than inferred from the disappearance of connected pores. High-temperature densification is compatible with this concept: its defining advance is control of final geometry together with density and mechanical performance.

The technical motivation is grounded in the effort to integrate ceramic shaping and densification. The supplied evidence review verified a subscription preview of a 2024 review of direct laser additive manufacturing, whose abstract identifies pores, cracks and reduced mechanical properties as continuing obstacles. That establishes a relevant manufacturing problem, while leaving the proposed combination of capabilities to be demonstrated.

significance.text: As a conditional consequence of the proposed capability, designers could specify both inaccessible internal geometry and finished functional surfaces in structural ceramics. An enclosed cooling passage, for example, could be formed during printing while its surrounding component retained the required dimensions after densification. This would expand the usable design space beyond shapes whose critical surfaces can all be reached by a grinding tool.

Potential applications include ceramic heat exchangers, cores and blades. These are downstream possibilities, not automatic outcomes of accurate printing: each would still require suitable surface quality, material compatibility, durability, reliability and manufacturing qualification. The breakthrough would not itself establish improved brittleness, oxidation resistance or fiber economics.

The analogy to printed-metal design freedom is useful only at the level of expanding geometric options. It does not establish equivalent feature sizes, surface finish, throughput, reliability or application readiness. The supplied evidence also does not substantiate the earlier assertion that grinding dominates the cost of hard ceramic parts. The defensible significance is the proposed combination of geometry and performance, without a quantified cost advantage or a demonstrated equivalence to metal additive manufacturing.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability targeted by this entry is repeatable integration of shaping, densification and dimensional control across more than one structural ceramic. A successful process family would need to retain complex features and functional tolerances while delivering density and strength comparable with conventional sintering of the same composition. Success in one material or one simple coupon would establish a narrower result.

For direct laser processing, the documented barriers include pore formation, cracking and the resulting loss of mechanical performance. The verified 2024 review describes these as obstacles to wider adoption. Only its subscription preview was retained, so the supplied evidence does not support a detailed account of their causes or establish how completely particular processing strategies overcome them.

Engineering synthesis: indirect printing must reconcile the printed body's binder and pore content with the material redistribution needed for densification. Removing binder and eliminating pore volume can change dimensions; spatially uneven change can undermine tolerances or damage complex features. The supplied research identifies these concerns, but its retained evidence does not establish their magnitude across indirect processes. Similarly, high melting temperatures and thermal shock are proposed explanations for direct-processing difficulties here, rather than mechanisms verified by the retained review passages.

A further engineering challenge is transferability. The proposed material set includes both oxides and non-oxides, so the demonstration must establish where a common process family works and which material-specific changes it requires. Dimensional accuracy, density, residual defects and strength must be controlled together; improving one metric alone would not establish the full capability.

current_state.text: The strongest inspected evidence in the supplied review is “A critical review of direct laser additive manufacturing ceramics,” published on 9 November 2024 in International Journal of Minerals, Metallurgy and Materials, volume 31, pages 2607–2626. Its abstract identifies pores, cracks and reduced mechanical properties in high-performance ceramics made by direct laser additive manufacturing, and states that further improvements are needed for wider adoption. The retained material is a subscription preview, not the full article; an untruncated page extraction does not remove that access limitation.

The supplied research attributes a sintering-related volumetric shrinkage range of 15–30% to “Ceramic matrix composite additive manufacturing: Defect formation, inheritance, and inhibition,” Journal of Alloys and Compounds 1047, dated 5 December 2025, article 184973. It also reports discussion of cracking when printing and sintering must meet tight tolerances. No source artifact was retained for this article, and the research did not download its full PDF. These are therefore reported findings that could not be verified in the supplied evidence review; the numerical range should not be generalized to all technical ceramics or printing routes.

A potentially important silica result is described in the supplied research: Wei-Cheng Chao, Yi-Hua Kao, Chien-Hua Chen and Ying-Chih Liao, “Ultralow-shrinkage ceramic fabrication via three-dimensional printing of high-solid-loading suspensions,” Additive Manufacturing 115, dated 5 January 2026, article 105051. The research attributes to its abstract an 83 vol% silica suspension, isotropic volumetric shrinkage below 6.5%, and approximately 100% relative density. No artifact was retained, so these quantities remain unverified within the supplied review. If confirmed, they would demonstrate a low-shrinkage, near-full-density silica result, but would not alone satisfy the selected structural-material scope.

The same silica research summary attributes to the authors a claim that earlier ceramics had not combined less than 30% volumetric shrinkage with greater than 99% relative density. This is an unverified author claim about prior literature, not an independently established boundary. The available evidence cannot rank the silica work as the strongest low-shrinkage demonstration across the field.

For structural zirconia, the supplied research describes Xinyu Xu, Yi Feng, Shihao Wang and Ruifang Guan, “Coupling regulation toward low shrinkage and high-performance zirconia by DLP additive manufacturing,” Journal of Alloys and Compounds 1077, dated 15 July 2026, article 189569. It reports relative density of 99.02 ± 0.21%, linear shrinkages of 19.3%, 19.5% and 20.9% along X, Y and Z, respectively, and bending strength of 611.54 MPa after sintering. These values could not be verified because no artifact was retained. Taken as reported, they illustrate high density alongside substantial dimensional change in one zirconia process, rather than proving that this pairing is unavoidable for structural oxides.

The reported silica shrinkage is volumetric, whereas the reported zirconia values are linear, so the percentages are not directly comparable. Neither result, as supplied, establishes final functional tolerances in a complex structural part without grinding. Large shrinkage by itself also does not decide whether a process is net shape: the relevant question is whether the final functional surfaces meet the specified tolerances.

The supplied evidence does not establish whether the complete capability had been achieved by 1 November 2026. The freshness record is empty, three listed sources lack retained artifacts, and the inspected review describes direct-laser challenges in 2024. These limitations leave present-day field-wide achievement unresolved; they neither establish achievement nor show that the reported later results are false. Reference titles mentioning net-shape work likewise cannot establish success or failure against this entry's proposed requirements.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: manufacture parts in at least two structural ceramics selected from alumina, zirconia, silicon carbide and silicon nitride using the same process family. Each part should contain an enclosed channel or similarly inaccessible feature. Report material-specific process changes so that the claimed transferability can be assessed. Two materials would demonstrate breadth across those cases, not universality across structural ceramics.
completion_criteria.label: One process family prints two structural ceramics with inaccessible features

completion_criteria.text: Proposed material-performance criteria: after densification, compare each printed material with a conventional sintered reference of the same composition using comparable density and strength measurements. Report relative density, residual porosity and strength variability. Closed porosity alone is insufficient because isolated pores may remain. Any practical interpretation of fully dense should state the measurement method, uncertainty and detection limits.
completion_criteria.label: Density and strength are compared with composition-matched sintered references

completion_criteria.text: Proposed dimensional criteria: define application tolerances before fabrication, measure dimensional change through processing, and show that final functional surfaces meet those tolerances without finish grinding. Assess inaccessible internal features as well as external dimensions. No universal shrinkage percentage is proposed; predictable dimensional change is acceptable only when the resulting part satisfies the functional requirements.
completion_criteria.label: Final functional surfaces meet predefined tolerances without finish grinding

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: repeat the demonstration across builds and specimens, report yield and variability, and seek independent replication. Establish the demonstrated ranges of part size, wall thickness, channel geometry, surface quality and process time. Application-specific service testing would be needed before claiming qualified heat exchangers or blades. These are proposed acceptance requirements, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Repeated builds demonstrate reproducibility and establish practical process boundaries

completion_criteria.text: A dense silica model would not meet the selected structural-material scope. A dense zirconia coupon would not meet the proposal if it lacked the required complex feature or if its final functional surfaces missed tolerance. Conversely, an approximately one-fifth linear shrinkage value alone is not a sufficient reason to exclude a process whose final dimensions and other requirements are convincingly demonstrated.
completion_criteria.label: Approximately one-fifth linear shrinkage does not disqualify otherwise qualifying parts

related_concepts.text: CRM-04, “Densification of arbitrary structural ceramics without a high-temperature furnace cycle,” has the closest overlap. From the supplied roster title, it concerns processing temperature and material breadth; CRM-11 concerns final geometry, density and strength together. A low-temperature, dimensionally accurate printing process might contribute to both. CRM-11 can also be satisfied using hot densification, while CRM-04's title does not itself require complex printed geometry. Only the roster title was supplied for this comparison.

CRM-01, room-temperature tensile ductility, and CRM-05, repeated restoration of strength after critical cracks, address mechanical behavior and damage recovery. CRM-11 seeks to preserve conventional material performance during complex shaping; it does not establish ductility or self-repair. CRM-12, large transparent ceramics with failure stress approaching theoretical strength, overlaps in its concern with density and defects, but adds optical, size and strength ambitions beyond this manufacturing proposal.

CRM-02, long service in air above the silica limit, and CRM-07, retention of heat transport after fusion-relevant irradiation, concern service environments. Accurate printing could enable useful component geometries for either, but would not establish oxidation resistance or irradiation tolerance. CRM-08 concerns industrial-cost stoichiometric silicon-carbide fiber and composites; geometric manufacturing capability does not resolve fiber production cost or composite performance.

CRM-03, ceramic electrolytes for lithium-metal cells; CRM-06, useful ambient-pressure, room-temperature ceramic superconductors; CRM-09, olefin–paraffin separation membranes; and CRM-10, practical solar water-to-fuel oxides, target distinct functional properties and system outcomes. Ceramic printing might assist component fabrication, but meeting CRM-11's structural density, strength and dimensional criteria would not establish their electrochemical, superconducting, separation or solar-fuel capabilities. These distinctions are synthesis from the supplied roster titles, not comparisons with full concept records.

change_log.change: Preserved CRM-11's identity and defined its endpoint as complex structural geometry, conventional sintered density and strength, and final functional tolerances without finish grinding.
change_log.reason: The review supports a coherent manufacturing objective; limitations in individual supporting assertions do not invalidate that objective.

change_log.change: Replaced literal zero-shrinkage and exact-density implications with functional tolerances and explicit density, porosity and measurement requirements.
change_log.reason: Nonzero dimensional change can be compatible with net shape, and closed porosity does not establish full density.

change_log.change: Retained the indirect-processing explanation as qualified engineering synthesis and separated it from verified direct-laser defect findings.
change_log.reason: The retained preview supports pores, cracks and mechanical-property limitations, but does not verify the broader shrinkage mechanisms or specific thermal explanations.

change_log.change: Preserved the reported composite-review, silica and zirconia numerical details, dates and scope while explicitly identifying their missing source artifacts.
change_log.reason: Useful research detail should remain available without being presented as independently verified evidence or rejected merely because verification was unavailable.

change_log.change: Removed claims of the strongest demonstration, inevitable density–shrinkage coupling and established field-wide nonachievement in 2026.
change_log.reason: The inspected 2024 preview and incomplete later-source record cannot support those rankings or present-day absence claims.

change_log.change: Qualified application and impact claims, including printed-metal design freedom and grinding-cost dominance.
change_log.reason: Geometric benefits follow conditionally from the proposed capability; cost dominance, equivalent design freedom and application readiness are not established.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed demonstrations to include matched references, predefined tolerances, reproducibility, uncertainty and practical operating boundaries.
change_log.reason: These make the endpoint assessable while preserving its status as a proposal and limiting conclusions to demonstrated breadth.

change_log.change: Replaced automatic exclusion based on approximately one-fifth zirconia shrinkage with an assessment of final tolerances and the complete demonstration.
change_log.reason: Shrinkage magnitude alone does not determine whether final dimensions meet functional requirements.

change_log.change: Used the supplied roster to explain overlaps and distinctions while identifying title-only comparisons.
change_log.reason: The roster permits a limited comparison, including with CRM-04, but does not supply detailed evidence about the other concepts.

unresolved_issues: The complete capability's achievement status as of 1 November 2026 remains unresolved because the supplied freshness record is empty and field coverage is incomplete.

The composite-review shrinkage range, silica suspension and densification results, and zirconia density, shrinkage and strength values require source verification; no artifacts were retained for those three articles.
The silica authors' reported prior-literature boundary and the ranking of low-shrinkage demonstrations remain unverified.

The review's recommendation to omit unverified numerical results was not adopted literally: the user requested preservation of useful quantitative research detail. Those results are retained as explicitly attributed reports with verification limitations.
Detailed mechanisms and magnitudes of indirect-process shrinkage, and the proposed thermal causes of direct-process defects, are not established by the retained review passages.
Application tolerances, density measurement limits, reference strength protocols, replication scope and acceptable manufacturing yield remain to be specified for an actual demonstration.
Comparisons with related concepts are limited to their supplied titles; detailed overlap with CRM-04 and the other entries remains unassessed.

brief.title: Printing strong ceramic parts ready to use
possible: Designers could make strong ceramic parts with enclosed cooling passages and surfaces accurate enough to use without grinding them to size. Even surfaces that tools cannot reach would meet the finished part’s requirements.
why: Ceramic heat exchangers and blades could take shapes that grinding tools cannot finish. Designers would gain more freedom to combine useful internal passages with the density and strength of conventionally made ceramics.

sources.who: Authors of the ceramic matrix composite manufacturing review
sources.showed: This review examines defects, shrinkage and cracking in printed ceramic composites.
sources.cited_for: It supports the concern that shrinkage and cracking complicate accurate ceramic printing.
sources.not_established: It does not establish a process that combines finished dimensions, complex geometry and conventional ceramic performance.

sources.who: Dake Zhao, Guijun Bi and colleagues
sources.showed: Their review identifies pores, cracks and reduced mechanical performance as continuing problems in ceramics printed directly with lasers.
sources.quote: However, high-performance ceramics fabricated by DLAM face challenges such as formation of pores and cracks and resultant low mechanical properties, hindering their practical application in high-end equipment.
sources.cited_for: It establishes defects and lost strength as barriers to direct laser printing of useful ceramic parts.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate complex parts that achieve the required density, strength and final dimensions together.

sources.who: Wei-Cheng Chao, Yi-Hua Kao, Chien-Hua Chen and Ying-Chih Liao
sources.showed: This study concerns printing silica from a mixture containing a high proportion of solid particles to limit shrinkage.
sources.cited_for: It supports the possibility of combining low shrinkage with near-full density in silica.
sources.not_established: Silica falls outside the selected structural ceramics, and the work does not establish finished functional dimensions in those materials.

sources.who: Xinyu Xu, Yi Feng, Shihao Wang and Ruifang Guan
sources.showed: This study examines shrinkage and mechanical performance in zirconia, a structural ceramic, printed using light.
sources.cited_for: It supports the possibility of dense, strong printed zirconia despite substantial shrinkage.
sources.not_established: It does not establish complex zirconia parts whose functional surfaces meet final tolerances without grinding.

shown: Chao and colleagues report silica close to full density with little shrinkage. Xu and colleagues report dense, strong zirconia with substantial shrinkage during sintering, the heating step that consolidates a ceramic.
missing: A shared printing approach must work across multiple structural ceramics while preserving enclosed features.
Printed parts must match conventionally sintered material in density and strength, with remaining pores measured.
Internal and external functional surfaces must meet specified dimensional limits without finish grinding.
Repeated builds and independent replication must establish reliability and practical manufacturing limits.

milestones.label: A shared process prints enclosed features in two ceramics
milestones.explanation: One process family would have to make enclosed features in two materials chosen from alumina, zirconia, silicon carbide and silicon nitride, with material-specific changes stated. This would establish transferability across those cases.

milestones.label: Density and strength match conventional references
milestones.explanation: Each material would need density, remaining pores and strength variability measured against conventionally sintered references of the same composition. This would establish performance beyond merely closing connected pores.

milestones.label: Finished surfaces meet predefined dimensional limits without grinding
milestones.explanation: Final internal and external functional surfaces would have to meet application limits set before fabrication, with dimensional changes measured. This would establish that the parts emerge at usable dimensions.

milestones.label: Repeated builds establish reliability and practical limits
milestones.explanation: Repeated builds would need consistent results, reported yield and variability, independent replication, and defined geometry, surface and timing limits. This would establish reproducibility and the process’s practical range.

milestones.label: Substantial shrinkage remains compatible with qualifying parts
milestones.explanation: A part shrinking by about one-fifth in length could still qualify if it met the material, geometry, performance and final dimensional requirements. This keeps success tied to usable parts rather than shrinkage alone.

uncertain: Whether any process already combines the complete set of capabilities remains unresolved.
Application limits, pore detection limits, strength comparisons and acceptable manufacturing yield still need precise definitions.
The extent to which a common process can span the selected ceramic materials remains open.

page.title: Net-shape additive manufacturing of fully dense technical ceramics
page.definition: Additive manufacturing produces technical-ceramic components with inaccessible internal features, full density and the required mechanical properties, while functional surfaces meet final dimensional tolerances without finish grinding. Full density means bulk density consistent with pore-free material, with residual porosity assessed separately.

goal.need: An alumina study published on 28 October 2024 found that flexural strength varied between manufacturing laboratories; its specimen count and failure analysis are tabulated below. A review identifies pores, cracks and reduced mechanical properties as obstacles in direct laser ceramic printing. The goal combines final dimensional conformity with material acceptance, including on surfaces inaccessible to grinding.

completion.title: Repeated builds yield fully dense ceramic parts meeting final tolerances without finish grinding.
completion.criterion: For a specified ceramic composition and component drawing, repeated builds produce components containing an enclosed channel or another feature inaccessible to finish grinding. After thermal processing, bulk density agrees with 100% of the composition's pore-free density within measurement uncertainty; no residual open or closed porosity is resolved at the application's specified detection limits; strength meets the acceptance criteria applied to conventionally sintered material of the same composition; and functional surfaces meet the drawing without finish grinding. Qualification follows the application's sampling plan.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no external body was found to have published this combined acceptance test.
completion.basis: NIST, NETL, the AMSC roadmap, ISO/ASTM 52957 and ISO/ASTM 52920 were searched for a combined density, strength and final-geometry acceptance test; none was found. ISO/ASTM 52920 provides a qualification framework rather than universal ceramic property limits. This fallback tests one composition and application at a time. The cited results do not establish achievement of the combined test.

milestones.title: A printed ceramic test piece reaches its composition's pore-free density within measurement uncertainty.
milestones.criterion: Bulk density agrees with 100% relative density within stated uncertainty, with open and closed pores assessed. ISO 18754 cautions that liquid displacement may be unsatisfactory below 0.5% open porosity. Kyocera lists typical printed alumina and zirconia densities of 3.9 and 6.0 g/cm³, without specimen counts or residual-porosity limits. Pelanconi et al., published on 17 September 2021, report 98.3% relative density for silicon-infiltrated SiC. Outside these cases, Chao et al., 5 January 2026, report silica at approximately 100% relative density with less than 6.5% volumetric shrinkage; the abstract gives no specimen count.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; ISO 18754 supplies density and apparent-porosity methods, but no universal full-density acceptance threshold for printed ceramics was found.

milestones.title: Printed ceramic specimens meet the strength limits applied to composition-matched conventional material.
milestones.criterion: Printed specimens meet the strength acceptance criteria applied to composition-matched conventionally sintered material under comparable geometry, surface condition and loading. Kyocera lists typical three-point flexural strengths of 460 MPa for printed alumina and 1000 MPa for printed zirconia; specimen counts are unspecified and these vendor data are not peer reviewed. Iyer et al., 25 February 2008, report silicon nitride with mechanical properties similar to conventional material; the abstract gives no specimen count. Pelanconi et al. measured 127 MPa biaxial strength for silicon-infiltrated SiC, with five specimens tested.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; searches of NIST, the AMSC roadmap and the ceramic design-standard sample found no cross-material numerical strength-equivalence criterion.

milestones.title: A ceramic component's inaccessible functional surfaces meet its drawing without finish grinding.
milestones.criterion: A component containing an enclosed channel or another inaccessible feature meets its application drawing after thermal processing, including internal dimensions and functional surface finish, without finish grinding. Kyocera lists representative as-fired tolerances for alumina and zirconia of ±0.100 mm, or ±1% for dimensions above 10 mm; no build statistics or internal-surface acceptance results are supplied. These values do not establish simultaneous full density, mechanical acceptance and internal dimensional conformity.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; NETL publishes dimensional compensation as a goal, but no external net-shape acceptance test covering inaccessible functional surfaces was found.

milestones.title: A ceramic AM process repeatedly produces specimens meeting its specified material requirements.
milestones.criterion: The ceramic manufacturing process repeatedly produces reference specimens meeting its specified material requirements, with process location and dispersion quantified under ISO/ASTM 52920:2023, clause 7.1. Clause 7.2 permits qualification for changing parts of the same material. This milestone establishes material-process repeatability; completion additionally requires repeated conformity of complex components without finish grinding.
milestones.set_by: ISO and ASTM International, ISO/ASTM 52920:2023, clauses 7.1–7.2; a material-independent qualification criterion applied here to ceramic reference specimens.
milestones.threshold_quote:
ensure that the additive system operations can produce parts
repeatable that meet specified requirements.

not_found: The final text of ISO/ASTM 52957:2026 could not be inspected; the accessible technical sample was its final draft.
The supplied composite-review and zirconia-study publisher pages could not be opened beyond search extracts.
No external criterion requiring one process family to qualify across multiple listed ceramics was found.
No application-independent acceptance values were found for density uncertainty, strength equivalence, final tolerances, build count or manufacturing yield.
